notes: Every generated probe is run through the PRODUCTION guardrails (services/orchestrator/guardrails.py) — the harness does not reimplement format, legality or relevance. What it adds on top is what the guardrails do not check: does the probe go after the signal that is actually missing, does it repeat one already asked, does it leak the rubric, and does it stay on the same scenario.

cases.question: Tell me about a time a customer was upset with you or your company. What did you do?
cases.answer: There was a customer who was really annoyed about a delivery that never showed up. I apologised and got it re-sent for her.
missing: names what they learned or changed

cases.question: Walk me through how you'd diagnose a customer who says the dashboard 'isn't loading'.
cases.answer: I'd ask what browser they're on and whether anyone else on their team is seeing it, then try to reproduce it on my side.

cases.question: A customer is shouting at you on a call. Walk me through what you do.
cases.answer: I let them finish, then I play their problem back in my own words and set a boundary if it turns personal.
missing: sets a boundary if it turns personal

cases.question: A customer asks for a refund two days outside the policy window. How do you handle it?
cases.answer: I'd look at the reason first and their history with us before I decided anything.
missing: knows the limit of their own authority
explains the decision without hiding behind policy
asked_already: What's the reason you'd be looking for?
cases.notes: A follow-up that re-asks what was already asked reads as not listening — worse than no follow-up.

cases.question: Tell me about a time you owned a problem end to end.
cases.answer: I picked up a ticket nobody wanted and saw it through to the end.
missing: names the concrete steps they took
asked_already: What made you pick that one up?

cases.question: How do you decide when something needs to go to a senior colleague?
cases.answer: Usually when I've been going in circles for a while.
asked_already: How long is 'a while' before you'd hand it over?
cases.notes: The second probe on the same item. It must go after the OTHER missing signal, not re-word the first.

cases.question: Tell me about a time a customer was upset with you or your company. What did you do?
cases.answer: I'd just try to help them out as best I can and stay calm.
missing: acknowledges the customer's feeling before fixing
names what they learned or changed
cases.notes: Almost nothing to pull on. The honest probe asks for a concrete instance; a probe that pretends there was detail here is worse than the authored fallback.

cases.question: A customer writes in and says they have explained this three times already to three different people. You're the fourth. What are the first words out of your mouth?
cases.answer: I'd apologise for the trouble and try to help them as best I can.
missing: signals they have read the history
cases.notes: This is also the recorded false positive that stemming fixed: the model writes 'apologizing' where the candidate said 'apologise', and exact-token relevance matching threw the probe away.

cases.question: A customer threatens to post about their problem on social media. What do you do?
cases.answer: I'd stay polite and try to sort it for them quickly.
missing: does not let the threat change the offer
flags it to the right people
cases.notes: A probe reciting 'do you let the threat change the offer?' hands the candidate the rubric and stops measuring anything.

cases.question: Walk me through how you'd diagnose a customer who says the dashboard 'isn't loading'.
cases.answer: I'd check whether it's just them or their whole team, since that tells me if it's an account thing or a wider outage.
missing: knows when to escalate with reproduction steps
cases.notes: A probe that jumps to a new scenario makes the answer unscorable against the question it was asked for.
